questions.question: Immediately following delivery, the uterine fundus is about 13.5 cm above the symphysis pubis. Over the following days, it decreases in height at approximately what rate, becoming a pelvic organ by the end of the second week?

options.D: It does not decrease until 6 weeks postpartum

questions.explanation: After remaining constant for the first 24 hours, the fundal height decreases by about 1.25 cm every 24 hours, so that the uterus becomes a pelvic organ (no longer palpable abdominally) by the end of the second week postpartum, with involution slowing thereafter until the uterus is near-normal size by 6 weeks.
questions.sourceChapter: Normal Puerperium — Clinical Assessment of Involution

questions.question: The reddish vaginal discharge seen in the first 1-4 days after delivery is called:
questions.explanation: Lochia progresses through three stages by colour: lochia rubra (red, days 1-4), lochia serosa (yellowish/pink/pale brownish, days 5-9), and lochia alba (pale white, days 10-15).
questions.sourceChapter: Normal Puerperium — Lochia

questions.question: Persistence of red-coloured lochia well beyond the normal expected duration most likely signifies:

options.A: Normal healing with no clinical concern
options.B: Subinvolution of the uterus or retained bits of the conceptus
options.C: A completely normal variant seen in all women
options.D: Onset of the first postpartum menstrual period

questions.explanation: Persistence of the red colour of lochia beyond the normal limit is a clinically important sign suggesting subinvolution of the uterus or retained products of conception, and should prompt further evaluation.
questions.sourceChapter: Normal Puerperium — Lochia, Clinical Importance

questions.question: Which hormone is chiefly responsible for the 'milk ejection' or 'let-down' reflex during breastfeeding?
questions.explanation: Oxytocin is the major galactokinetic hormone: suckling triggers a neural reflex arc to the hypothalamus, causing oxytocin release from the posterior pituitary, which contracts the myoepithelial cells around the alveoli and ducts, forcing milk down into the lactiferous ducts (the 'let-down' reflex). Prolactin, by contrast, drives milk secretion itself (lactogenesis/galactopoiesis), not its ejection.
questions.sourceChapter: Normal Puerperium — Physiology of Lactation, Galactokinesis

questions.question: Although prolactin levels are high throughout pregnancy, actual milk secretion does not begin until around the 3rd-4th postpartum day. What explains this delay?

options.A: Prolactin has no role in milk secretion at all
options.B: High circulating estrogen and progesterone during pregnancy make breast tissue unresponsive to prolactin; their withdrawal after delivery allows prolactin to act
options.C: The breasts are not anatomically ready until several days after birth
options.D: Oxytocin blocks prolactin receptors until labour is complete

questions.explanation: During pregnancy, the high circulating levels of estrogen and progesterone keep the fully-developed mammary glands unresponsive to prolactin, holding milk secretion in abeyance despite high prolactin levels. Once these steroids fall sharply after delivery, prolactin is free to begin its secretory (lactogenic) action.
questions.sourceChapter: Normal Puerperium — Physiology of Lactation, Lactogenesis

questions.question: According to the objectives of postpartum exercise, which muscle groups are specifically targeted to prevent genital prolapse and stress incontinence of urine?

options.B: The abdominal and pelvic floor muscles

questions.explanation: Postpartum exercises aim to improve tone of the abdominal and perineal (pelvic floor) muscles, which are stretched during pregnancy and labour. Effective pelvic floor exercise specifically helps prevent genital prolapse and stress urinary incontinence.
questions.sourceChapter: Normal Puerperium — Postpartum Exercise

questions.question: How long should postpartum exercises generally be continued for maximal benefit, per standard obstetric guidance?

options.A: Only for the first 24 hours after delivery
options.C: Only once, on the day of discharge
options.D: Postpartum exercise is not recommended at all

questions.explanation: Postpartum exercises — breathing exercises, leg movements, and toning of abdominal, pelvic floor, and back muscles — should be continued for at least 3 months, and are ideally taught by a trained physiotherapist.
questions.sourceChapter: Normal Puerperium — Postpartum Exercise

questions.question: 'Subinvolution' and 'superinvolution' of the uterus refer respectively to:

options.A: Delayed/incomplete involution, and a smaller-than-normal uterus sometimes seen with continued lactation
options.B: Two names for exactly the same clinical finding
options.C: Involution occurring only in the cervix versus only in the vagina
options.D: Terms with no real clinical distinction from normal involution

questions.explanation: Subinvolution refers to involution proceeding more slowly or incompletely than expected. Superinvolution, by contrast, describes a uterus that becomes smaller than normal, sometimes seen in lactating women — a change that reverses if lactation is withheld.
questions.sourceChapter: Normal Puerperium — Clinical Assessment of Involution

questions.question: Early ambulation after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery is encouraged mainly because it:

options.A: Has no measurable benefit but is traditional practice
options.B: Reduces bladder complications and constipation, facilitates uterine drainage, and lessens the risk of puerperal venous thrombosis and embolism
options.D: Prevents postpartum haemorrhage entirely on its own

questions.explanation: Early ambulation after delivery provides a sense of well-being, reduces bladder complications and constipation, facilitates uterine drainage (hastening involution), and importantly lessens the risk of puerperal venous thrombosis and embolism.
questions.sourceChapter: Normal Puerperium — Management, Rest and Ambulation

questions.question: Compared to mature breast milk, colostrum has:

options.A: Lower protein but higher fat and carbohydrate content
options.B: Higher protein content but lower fat and carbohydrate content
options.C: Identical composition to mature milk in every respect

questions.explanation: Colostrum has a notably higher protein content than mature breast milk, but lower fat and carbohydrate content. It also contains locally-produced antibody (IgA), providing important early immunological protection to the newborn.
questions.sourceChapter: Normal Puerperium — Lactation, Composition of Colostrum

questions.question: Exclusive breastfeeding provides approximately what level of contraceptive protection for the first 6 months postpartum?
questions.explanation: In a woman who is exclusively breastfeeding, lactational amenorrhoea provides approximately 98% contraceptive protection for up to 6 months postpartum — a recognised natural method of contraception, though ovulation can occasionally precede the return of menstruation.
questions.sourceChapter: Normal Puerperium — Menstruation and Ovulation

questions.question: A postnatal patient reports backache localized specifically over the lumbar region (rather than the sacrum). This location most likely points to:

options.B: An orthopedic condition, which is often relieved by physiotherapy
options.C: It always indicates retained products of conception
options.D: It is never a genuine finding after delivery

questions.explanation: Postnatal backache over the sacrum is more likely due to pelvic pathology, while backache over the lumbar region is more likely due to an orthopedic cause, and is often relieved by physiotherapy.
questions.sourceChapter: Normal Puerperium — Postnatal Care, Management of Ailments

questions.question: In the first week postpartum, there is a secondary increase in fibrinogen, factor VIII, and platelets. What clinical risk does this hypercoagulable state primarily raise?
questions.explanation: The secondary rise in fibrinogen, factor VIII, and platelet count (with increased platelet adhesiveness) during the first postpartum week increases the risk of thrombosis — one reason early ambulation and postpartum exercise are actively encouraged, since enhanced fibrinolytic activity in the first few days acts as a partial protective counter-mechanism.
questions.sourceChapter: Normal Puerperium — Blood Values

questions.question: A woman who delivers twins in her first pregnancy is correctly recorded as:
questions.explanation: Gravida and para refer to PREGNANCIES, not the number of babies delivered. A woman delivering twins in her first pregnancy is still gravida one, para one — parity is not increased by multiple fetuses in a single pregnancy.
questions.sourceChapter: Antenatal Care — History Taking, Vital Statistics

questions.question: A woman having her first pregnancy at what age or older is termed an 'elderly primigravida' (per FIGO)?
questions.explanation: A woman having her first pregnancy at age 30 or above is generally termed elderly primigravida in clinical practice, though FIGO specifically sets the threshold at 35 years. Extremes of maternal age (teenage and elderly) are recognised obstetric risk factors.
questions.sourceChapter: Antenatal Care — History Taking, Vital Statistics

questions.question: A pregnant woman with a history of four or more previous births is termed:
questions.explanation: A woman with a previous history of four or more births is called a grand multipara — distinct from nullipara (never completed a pregnancy to viability) and primipara (has delivered exactly one viable child).
questions.sourceChapter: Antenatal Care — History Taking, Terminology

questions.question: According to standard antenatal care guidance, the first antenatal visit should not be deferred beyond:
questions.explanation: The first antenatal visit should not be deferred beyond the second missed menstrual period — it may occur even earlier if the patient is considering termination of the pregnancy.
questions.sourceChapter: Antenatal Care — Procedure at the First Visit

questions.question: Per the criteria described for a 'normal pregnancy', delivery is expected to occur at term (between 38-42 weeks) with a fetal weight of at least:

options.D: Weight is not part of the criteria

questions.explanation: The criteria for a 'normal pregnancy' include delivery of a single baby in good condition at term (38-42 weeks), with a fetal weight of 2.5 kg or more, and with no maternal complications — making 'normal pregnancy' technically a retrospective classification.
questions.sourceChapter: Antenatal Care — Aims and Objectives

questions.question: The 'plane of least pelvic dimensions' (narrow pelvic plane), a landmark used for pudendal nerve block, corresponds anatomically to approximately the level of:

options.D: The pubic symphysis alone, excluding any posterior landmark

questions.explanation: The plane of least pelvic dimensions extends from the lower border of the symphysis pubis to the tip of the ischial spines, and posteriorly to the 5th sacral vertebra. It is the narrowest plane in the pelvis, roughly corresponds to the origin of levator ani, is where internal rotation of the fetal head occurs, and is the landmark used for pudendal nerve block.
questions.sourceChapter: Fetal Skull and Maternal Pelvis — Outlet

questions.question: The physiological relaxation of the pelvic joints (symphysis pubis and sacroiliac joints) during pregnancy is primarily attributed to which hormones?
questions.explanation: Relaxation of the pelvic joints during pregnancy — increased width and mobility of the symphysis pubis, and similar changes in the sacroiliac joints — is attributed to the hormones progesterone and relaxin, facilitating the anteroposterior diameter increase needed during labor.
questions.sourceChapter: Fetal Skull and Maternal Pelvis — Physiological Enlargement of Pelvis
